blocks.text: Matrices and types of matrices

A **matrix** is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns, enclosed in brackets. Matrices store data compactly (marks of students in several subjects, prices of items in several shops) and let us solve many equations at once. A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns has **order** $m \times n$ (read "m by n") and contains $mn$ entries. The entry in the $i$-th row and $j$-th column is written $a_{ij}$, so a matrix can be written $A=[a_{ij}]_{m\times n}$.

An ordered rectangular array of numbers (real numbers in this course) arranged in $m$ rows and $n$ columns. Its order is $m\times n$, and it has $m\times n$ elements. Two matrices are of the same order only if both their numbers of rows and their numbers of columns match.

To build a matrix from a rule, substitute each $(i,j)$ into the rule. For a $2\times 2$ matrix with $a_{ij}=i+2j$ we get $a_{11}=3$, $a_{12}=5$, $a_{21}=4$, $a_{22}=6$, so $A=\begin{bmatrix}3&5\\4&6\end{bmatrix}$. If a matrix has 12 elements, its possible orders are the factor pairs of 12: $1\times12,\ 12\times1,\ 2\times6,\ 6\times2,\ 3\times4,\ 4\times3$ (six orders).

rows: Square; all entries below / above the diagonal are 0

blocks.text: Every identity matrix is scalar and every scalar matrix is diagonal, but not the other way round. $\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&5\end{bmatrix}$ is diagonal but **not** scalar because its diagonal entries differ.
Equality, transpose, symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
Two matrices $A=[a_{ij}]$ and $B=[b_{ij}]$ are equal if (i) they have the same order and (ii) $a_{ij}=b_{ij}$ for every $i,j$. Equating corresponding entries gives equations in the unknowns.
If $\begin{bmatrix}x+y&2\\3&x-y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7&2\\3&1\end{bmatrix}$ then $x+y=7$ and $x-y=1$, so $x=4$, $y=3$.
The transpose $A^{T}$ (or $A'$) of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ is the $n\times m$ matrix obtained by interchanging rows and columns, so $(A^T)_{ij}=a_{ji}$.
$k$ is a scalar. The last rule **reverses the order** of the product; it is valid whenever $AB$ is defined.

A square matrix $A$ is **symmetric** if $A^T=A$, i.e. $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$. It is **skew-symmetric** if $A^T=-A$, i.e. $a_{ij}=-a_{ji}$. Putting $i=j$ in the second condition gives $a_{ii}=-a_{ii}$, so every diagonal entry of a skew-symmetric matrix is 0.

For any square matrix $A$, the matrix $A+A^T$ is symmetric and $A-A^T$ is skew-symmetric. Hence $A=\tfrac12(A+A^T)+\tfrac12(A-A^T)$ is the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix, and this split is unique.

blocks.problem: Write $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&6\\2&8\end{bmatrix}$ as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.

blocks.text: Algebra of matrices

**Addition and subtraction** are done entry by entry and only for matrices of the **same order**. **Scalar multiplication** $kA$ multiplies every entry by $k$. Addition is commutative and associative, $O$ is the additive identity, and $-A$ is the additive inverse of $A$.

If $A$ is $m\times n$ and $B$ is $n\times p$, the product $AB$ is the $m\times p$ matrix whose $(i,k)$ entry is $\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}b_{jk}$ (row $i$ of $A$ times column $k$ of $B$). $AB$ exists only when the number of columns of $A$ equals the number of rows of $B$.

What to learn from this figure: the entry in row i, column k of AB uses only row i of A and column k of B, multiplying matching entries and adding. The two matching lengths (3 columns of A, 3 rows of B) are why the product exists, and the outer numbers 2 and 2 give the order of AB.

blocks.answer: The null matrix $O$ (this is the Cayley-Hamilton relation $\lambda^2-2\lambda+3=0$ for $A$).

blocks.text: Properties: $A(BC)=(AB)C$, $A(B+C)=AB+AC$, $AI=IA=A$. But matrix multiplication is **not commutative** ($AB\ne BA$ in general), $AB=O$ does not force $A=O$ or $B=O$, and $(A+B)^2\neq A^2+2AB+B^2$ unless $AB=BA$.

Always check orders first: a $3\times2$ matrix times a $2\times4$ matrix gives $3\times4$; the reverse product $2\times4$ times $3\times2$ is not defined. Multiply row by column, never entry by entry.
Determinants

Every square matrix $A$ has a number $|A|$ (also $\det A$). For $A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}$, $|A|=ad-bc$. For a $3\times3$ matrix, expand along a row or column using minors and cofactors: $|A|=a_{11}C_{11}+a_{12}C_{12}+a_{13}C_{13}$, where $C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$ and $M_{ij}$ is the minor (determinant left after deleting row $i$ and column $j$).

blocks.text: A square matrix is **singular** if $|A|=0$ and **non-singular** if $|A|\neq0$. Only non-singular matrices have an inverse.

What to learn from this figure: for a 2 by 2 matrix, ad - bc measures the area of the parallelogram formed by its two columns. When the columns lie along one line the area collapses to 0, which is exactly the singular case |A| = 0 that has no inverse. (The area picture is extra intuition; the exam uses the ad - bc rule.)
$|A+B|\neq|A|+|B|$ in general, and $|kA|=k^n|A|$, not $k|A|$. For a $3\times3$ matrix, $|2A|=8|A|$.
Inverse of a matrix
A square matrix $A$ is **invertible** if there is a matrix $B$ of the same order with $AB=BA=I$; then $B=A^{-1}$ is unique. $A^{-1}$ exists exactly when $|A|\neq0$.

$\operatorname{adj}A$ is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors $C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$. For a $2\times2$ matrix, $\operatorname{adj}\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}$. Also $A\,\operatorname{adj}A=|A|I$.
Valid when $A$ and $B$ are invertible square matrices of the same size. The first result reverses the order, like the transpose rule.

blocks.solution:
$|A|=2\cdot4-3\cdot1=5\neq0$, so the inverse exists.

$\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{bmatrix}4&-3\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$.

$A^{-1}=\tfrac15\begin{bmatrix}4&-3\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$.

Check: first row of $A$ times first column of $\operatorname{adj}A$: $2\cdot4+3(-1)=5$, so $AA^{-1}$ has entry 1 there.

blocks.text: For an $n\times n$ invertible $A$: $|A^{-1}|=1/|A|$ and $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}$.
Solving simultaneous equations using the matrix method
A system of linear equations in two or three unknowns can be written as $AX=B$, where $A$ is the coefficient matrix, $X$ the column of unknowns and $B$ the column of constants.

If $|A|\neq0$ the system is **consistent with a unique solution** $X=A^{-1}B$. If $|A|=0$, compute $(\operatorname{adj}A)B$: if it is the zero matrix the system has infinitely many solutions; if it is not zero the system is inconsistent (no solution).

What to learn from this figure: |A| not equal to 0 means the lines cross once (unique solution). If |A| = 0, the lines are parallel or the same line, and the test (adj A)B decides: not zero means parallel (no solution), zero means the same line (infinitely many).

blocks.problem: Solve $x+y+z=6,\ x-y+z=2,\ 2x+y-z=1$ by the matrix method.
blocks.solution:
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\1&-1&1\\2&1&-1\end{bmatrix}$, $|A|=1(1-1)-1(-1-2)+1(1+2)=6\neq0$.

Cofactors give $\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{bmatrix}0&2&2\\3&-3&0\\3&1&-2\end{bmatrix}$, so $X=\tfrac16\operatorname{adj}A\begin{bmatrix}6\\2\\1\end{bmatrix}=\tfrac16\begin{bmatrix}0+4+2\\18-6+0\\18+2-2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{bmatrix}$.

Check in equation 3: $2(1)+2-3=1$. Correct.

blocks.text: Substitute your answer back into **all** equations. A common error is a sign slip in one cofactor; one failed check shows it immediately.
Remember: write $AX=B$; find $|A|$; if non-zero, $X=A^{-1}B=\frac{1}{|A|}(\operatorname{adj}A)B$; if zero, test $(\operatorname{adj}A)B$.

questions.stem: A matrix has 12 elements. How many different orders can it have?
questions.explanation: Orders are ordered pairs $(m,n)$ with $mn=12$. The factor pairs are $1\times12$, $12\times1$, $2\times6$, $6\times2$, $3\times4$ and $4\times3$, since $m\times n$ and $n\times m$ are different orders. That gives 6 possible orders.

optionRationale.2: Counts only the orders with $m\le n$; $3\times4$ and $4\times3$ are different orders.
optionRationale.3: Counts only the factor pairs $1,2,3,4$ ignoring the reversed ones.
optionRationale.4: 12 is the number of elements, not the number of possible orders.

questions.objective: Count the possible orders of a matrix from its number of elements

questions.stem: A $2\times2$ matrix $A=[a_{ij}]$ is defined by $a_{ij}=2i-j$. The sum of all its elements is
questions.explanation: Substitute: $a_{11}=2-1=1$, $a_{12}=2-2=0$, $a_{21}=4-1=3$, $a_{22}=4-2=2$. The matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\3&2\end{bmatrix}$ and the sum of its elements is $1+0+3+2=6$.

optionRationale.1: Takes $a_{12}=2$ instead of 0 or misses one entry.
optionRationale.3: Obtained by wrongly adding $j$ instead of subtracting it for some entries; the rule is $2i-j$.

questions.objective: Construct a matrix from a rule for its elements

questions.stem: A square matrix in which every non-diagonal element is 0 and all diagonal elements are equal to 5 is called a
options: diagonal matrix that is not scalar
questions.explanation: A diagonal matrix has zero off-diagonal entries. When the diagonal entries are all the same non-zero number (here 5) it is a scalar matrix, namely $5I$. It is not the identity matrix because the diagonal entry is 5, not 1.

optionRationale.1: An identity matrix needs the common diagonal entry to be 1, not 5.
optionRationale.2: The diagonal entries are all equal, so it is scalar.
optionRationale.4: A null matrix has every entry 0, including the diagonal.

questions.objective: Identify scalar and identity matrices

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Every diagonal element of a skew-symmetric matrix is zero.
Reason (R): For a skew-symmetric matrix $a_{ij}=-a_{ji}$ for all $i,j$, so $a_{ii}=-a_{ii}$.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Skew-symmetry means $A^T=-A$, i.e. $a_{ij}=-a_{ji}$. Taking $i=j$ gives $a_{ii}=-a_{ii}$, so $2a_{ii}=0$ and $a_{ii}=0$. Hence both statements are true and the reason is exactly why the assertion holds.

optionRationale.2: The reason is the direct proof of the assertion, so it is the correct explanation.
optionRationale.3: The assertion is true: the diagonal of a skew-symmetric matrix is always zero.
optionRationale.4: The reason is true because $a_{ii}=-a_{ii}$ forces $a_{ii}=0$.

questions.objective: Prove that the diagonal of a skew-symmetric matrix is zero

questions.stem: If $\begin{bmatrix}x+y&2\\3&x-y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7&2\\3&1\end{bmatrix}$, then $xy$ equals
questions.explanation: Equal matrices have equal entries, so $x+y=7$ and $x-y=1$. Adding gives $2x=8$, so $x=4$, and then $y=3$. Therefore $xy=4\times3=12$.

optionRationale.2: Obtained from $x=5,\ y=2$, which does not satisfy $x-y=1$.
optionRationale.3: Obtained from $x=7,\ y=2$, which does not satisfy $x-y=1$.

questions.objective: Use equality of matrices to find unknowns

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$. The entry in the first row and second column of $(AB)^T$ is
questions.explanation: First $AB=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot0+2\cdot1&1\cdot1+2\cdot0\\3\cdot0+4\cdot1&3\cdot1+4\cdot0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&3\end{bmatrix}$. Transposing swaps the off-diagonal entries, giving $\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$, so the (1,2) entry is 4. This also equals the (1,2) entry of $B^TA^T$.

optionRationale.1: This is the (1,2) entry of $AB$ itself, before taking the transpose.

questions.objective: Apply the transpose to a matrix product

questions.stem: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\5&7\end{bmatrix}$, the element in the first row and second column of the symmetric matrix $\tfrac12(A+A^T)$ is
questions.explanation: $A^T=\begin{bmatrix}1&5\\3&7\end{bmatrix}$, so $A+A^T=\begin{bmatrix}2&8\\8&14\end{bmatrix}$ and half of it is $\begin{bmatrix}1&4\\4&7\end{bmatrix}$. The (1,2) element is $\tfrac12(3+5)=4$.

optionRationale.2: This is $a_{12}$ of $A$, not of the symmetric part.
optionRationale.4: This is $a_{21}$ of $A$, not of the symmetric part.

questions.objective: Find the symmetric part of a square matrix

questions.stem: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$, the element in the first row and second column of $A^5$ is
questions.explanation: Compute $A^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&4\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $A^3=A^2A=\begin{bmatrix}1&6\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. The pattern is $A^n=\begin{bmatrix}1&2n\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$, so $A^5$ has top-right entry $2\times5=10$.

optionRationale.1: Adds 1 five times instead of 2 five times.
optionRationale.2: Takes $2^5$, but the entry grows linearly, not exponentially.

questions.objective: Find powers of a matrix using a pattern

questions.stem: Matrices $A,\ B,\ C$ have orders $3\times2,\ 2\times4,\ 4\times1$ respectively. The order of the product $ABC$ is
questions.explanation: $AB$ is defined because $A$ has 2 columns and $B$ has 2 rows, giving a $3\times4$ matrix. Then $(AB)C$ is defined since 4 columns match the 4 rows of $C$, and the result has 3 rows and 1 column, so it is $3\times1$.

optionRationale.2: This is the order of $AB$ only.
optionRationale.3: Takes the inner orders instead of the outer ones.

questions.objective: Find the order of a matrix product

questions.stem: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\3&0\end{bmatrix}$, then $A^2-2A+3I$ is equal to
questions.explanation: $A^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\6&-3\end{bmatrix}$ and $2A=\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\6&0\end{bmatrix}$, so $A^2-2A=\begin{bmatrix}-3&0\\0&-3\end{bmatrix}=-3I$. Adding $3I$ gives the zero matrix.
questions.objective: Evaluate a matrix polynomial

questions.stem: The value of the determinant $\begin{vmatrix}6&-2\\-3&4\end{vmatrix}$ is
questions.explanation: For a $2\times2$ determinant $ad-bc$: $6\times4-(-2)\times(-3)=24-6=18$. The cross term is subtracted, and because $(-2)(-3)=+6$ the second product lowers 24 to 18.

optionRationale.1: Adds the cross product instead of subtracting: $24+6$.

questions.objective: Evaluate a 2x2 determinant

questions.stem: If $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix with $|A|=5$, then $|2A|$ equals
questions.explanation: Multiplying every row by 2 multiplies the determinant by $2$ three times, so $|2A|=2^3|A|=8\times5=40$. In general $|kA|=k^n|A|$ for an $n\times n$ matrix.

optionRationale.1: Uses $|2A|=2|A|$, which is wrong for a $3\times3$ matrix.
optionRationale.3: Uses $5^2$, unrelated to the scalar factor.

questions.objective: Use the scalar property of determinants

questions.stem: The matrix $\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&8&k\end{bmatrix}$ is singular when $k$ equals
questions.explanation: Expanding along the first row: $1(5k-48)-2(4k-42)+3(32-35)=5k-48-8k+84-9=27-3k$. A singular matrix has $|A|=0$, so $27-3k=0$ and $k=9$. This agrees with the pattern that rows $1,2,3$ are in arithmetic progression when $k=9$.
questions.objective: Find the value that makes a matrix singular

questions.stem: If $A$ and $B$ are $3\times3$ matrices with $|A|=-2$ and $|B|=5$, then $|2AB|$ equals
questions.explanation: First $|AB|=|A||B|=(-2)(5)=-10$. For a $3\times3$ matrix the scalar 2 contributes $2^3=8$, so $|2AB|=8\times(-10)=-80$. Using $2|AB|=-20$ would be wrong, because all three rows are multiplied by 2.
questions.objective: Combine |AB|=|A||B| with the scalar property

questions.stem: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&4\end{bmatrix}$, the element in the first row and second column of $A^{-1}$ is
questions.explanation: $|A|=2\cdot4-3\cdot1=5$ and $\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{bmatrix}4&-3\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$, so $A^{-1}=\tfrac15\begin{bmatrix}4&-3\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$. The (1,2) element is $-3/5$.

optionRationale.2: This is the entry of $\operatorname{adj}A$ in position (2,1) divided by $|A|$.

questions.objective: Find the inverse of a 2x2 matrix using the adjoint

questions.stem: If $A$ and $B$ are invertible square matrices of the same order, then $\left((AB)^T\right)^{-1}$ equals
questions.explanation: Use $(X^T)^{-1}=(X^{-1})^T$ with $X=AB$, and $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$. Then $((AB)^T)^{-1}=(B^{-1}A^{-1})^T$. Transposing a product reverses the order, so this equals $(A^{-1})^T(B^{-1})^T$.

optionRationale.2: Ignores both the transpose and the reversal of order.

questions.objective: Combine inverse and transpose properties

questions.stem: Let $A$ be a $3\times3$ matrix with $|A|=4$. Then $|\operatorname{adj}A|\cdot|A^{-1}|$ equals
questions.explanation: For an $n\times n$ matrix $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}$, so here $|\operatorname{adj}A|=4^2=16$. Also $|A^{-1}|=1/|A|=\tfrac14$. The product is $16\times\tfrac14=4$.
questions.objective: Use determinant properties of adjoint and inverse

questions.stem: The solution of $2x+y=5,\ x+3y=5$ is $(x,y)$. The value of $x^2+y^2$ is
questions.explanation: Here $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$, $|A|=5$, $A^{-1}=\tfrac15\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}$. Then $X=A^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}5\\5\end{bmatrix}=\tfrac15\begin{bmatrix}10\\5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}$. So $x^2+y^2=4+1=5$.

optionRationale.1: Obtained from $(3,0)$, which does not satisfy $x+3y=5$.
optionRationale.4: Obtained from $(3,2)$, which satisfies neither equation.

questions.objective: Solve a 2x2 system by the matrix method

questions.stem: If $x+y+z=6,\ x-y+z=2,\ 2x+y-z=1$, then $x+2y+3z$ equals
questions.explanation: Add the first two equations: $2x+2z=8$ so $x+z=4$. Subtracting gives $2y=4$, so $y=2$. The third equation gives $2x-z=1-y=-1$. Adding $x+z=4$ gives $3x=3$, $x=1$, $z=3$. Then $x+2y+3z=1+4+9=14$. (The determinant of coefficients is 6, so the solution is unique.)

optionRationale.1: Obtained by a slip that gives $z=2.5$ with the other values correct; it does not satisfy the equations.
optionRationale.2: Obtained from $(x,y,z)=(1,2,2)$, which fails the first equation $x+y+z=6$.
optionRationale.4: Obtained from $(x,y,z)=(2,2,3)$, which fails the first equation.

questions.objective: Solve a 3-variable system and evaluate an expression

questions.stem: For the system $x+2y=3,\ 2x+4y=k$, the number of solutions is infinite when $k$ equals
questions.explanation: The coefficient matrix has $|A|=4-4=0$. Compute $(\operatorname{adj}A)B=\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-2&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3\\k\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}12-2k\\k-6\end{bmatrix}$. This is the zero matrix only for $k=6$, giving infinitely many solutions. For other $k$ the system is inconsistent.

optionRationale.1: With $k=3$ the second equation is $x+2y=1.5$, which contradicts the first.
optionRationale.2: With $k=12$ the second equation is $x+2y=6$, which contradicts the first.
optionRationale.3: With $k=0$ the second equation is $x+2y=0$, which contradicts the first.

questions.objective: Test consistency of a system when |A| = 0

questions.stem: Match each matrix in List-I with its description in List-II.
questions.explanation: A has unequal diagonal entries 3 and 5 with zeros elsewhere, so it is diagonal but not scalar (III). B satisfies $B^T=-B$ (I). C has 1 on the diagonal (II). D has $a_{12}=2\neq a_{21}=3$, so it is not symmetric, and its diagonal is non-zero, so it is not skew-symmetric (IV).

optionRationale.2: This mixes up the roles of A and B; A is diagonal and B is skew-symmetric.
optionRationale.3: The identity matrix has 1s on the diagonal and D is not an identity matrix.
optionRationale.4: A has unequal diagonal entries, so it cannot be the identity matrix, and D is not diagonal at all.

questions.objective: Classify matrices by type

right: III. Diagonal matrix that is not scalar

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about determinants.
A. A determinant with two identical rows has value 0.
B. Interchanging two rows changes the sign of the determinant.
C. $|A+B|=|A|+|B|$ for all square matrices of the same order.
D. Multiplying one row by $k$ multiplies the determinant by $k$.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A is true (subtracting the identical rows gives a zero row). B is true (a row interchange reverses the sign). D is true (a common factor of one row can be taken out). C is false: for $A=B=I_2$, $|A+B|=4$ but $|A|+|B|=2$.

optionRationale.2: This omits D, which is also a correct property.
optionRationale.3: C is false, so any option containing C is wrong.
optionRationale.4: C is false, so this option is wrong.

questions.objective: Recall elementary properties of determinants
